title: Stanford violated its AI policy by turning a Hispanic student into a fake Black woman in ad

reading.body:
This is a case of a generative image tool used to alter a photograph of real, identifiable people for promotional material, and of that altered image being published without disclosure. The failure sits in the production of marketing assets, not in a model making a claim or a decision. The tool did what such tools do: it produced a plausible image of a person who was not there, and the output was treated as usable artwork rather than as a fabricated depiction of a named student.

The institution had a rule that covered exactly this use, and the rule was not applied at the point where the image was made or approved. Catching it would have required a check at two places: a review step that asked whether the source photograph contained real students, and a disclosure step that flagged the edit to viewers. Neither the alteration nor the omission was caught before the banners went up.

What is not established is who operated the tool, what instructions were given, and whether anyone intended the substitution. The university has confirmed the edit and the policy breach, and has said it will add training and review, but no finding has been made about individual responsibility or intent.

reports.title: Stanford Used A.I. to Swap Black Student for Hispanic Student in a Photo
Stanford R&DE Uses AI to Race Swap Students for Advertising
University confirms use of AI-edited photo amid controversy
Stanford violated its AI policy by turning a Hispanic student into a fake Black woman in ad

summary:
Billy Ramirez, a Hispanic senior at Stanford University studying human biology, was photographed at a Lunar New Year party in 2024 alongside two other students. When Stanford reused the image on campus banners last week, an artificial intelligence tool had replaced Ramirez with a Black woman, and the other students' appearances were altered to look thinner. Ramirez learned about the change from a friend and said being erased so easily was upsetting.

Stanford acknowledged on Tuesday that it used AI to alter the original photo. The university said its policy strictly prohibits using AI to produce or change images of Stanford people, events, research, facilities or achievements, and that both the alteration and the failure to disclose it violated that policy. Stanford said it is working with Residential and Dining Enterprises to provide additional training and ensure proper review of all materials.
